item.title: The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too
item.description:
The Yemen war is not just Saudi Arabia’s problem. It’s the Gulf’s too Expert comment thilton.drupal 14 October 2026

The renewed conflict in Yemen exposes the limits of Saudi Arabia’s military options and the vulnerabilities of the Gulf states. A unified Gulf Cooperation Council strategy on Yemen and a credible political settlement between Yemenis are needed.

The Yemen conflict has escalated significantly in recent weeks. Houthi strikes on airports in Riyadh, Abha and Dammam have killed at least 20 people and injured hundreds. Saudi oil infrastructure has also been attacked. Within Yemen, renewed fighting following a Houthi offensive around the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait has brought return to full-scale war. 

The escalation is an alarming reminder of the 2015 Saudi-led intervention in Yemen. This came after the Iran-backed Houthis seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in September 2014 and ousted the internationally recognized government from power. More than a decade later, the Houthis remain entrenched and clearly emboldened, while Yemen’s government is fragmented. Prospects for a political settlement currently seem remote. 

Since the UN-brokered truce in April 2022, Saudi Arabia has sought to disengage militarily from Yemen and pursue a negotiated settlement with the Houthis. Talks gained momentum in 2023, but the Houthis’ involvement in the Gaza war, including attacks on Red Sea shipping and Israel, disrupted the political process. US president Donald Trump’s intensive bombing campaign against the Houthis led to a separate US-Houthi ceasefire in May 2025. But it did not advance solutions to the conflict in Yemen.

Difficult choices for Riyadh

Saudi Arabia now faces a difficult choice between flawed options.

The first option is military escalation through renewed air strikes and an offensive by Yemeni government-aligned forces. But this risks returning Riyadh to the costly, ill-planned and ill-conducted war it has spent years attempting to extricate itself from. 

The Houthis have learned that even limited strikes can impose disproportionate economic and political costs. This gives the group leverage that Saudi Arabia’s conventional military superiority has struggled to overcome.

Seeking to contain the Houthis has also proved insufficient. Although the relative calm following the 2022 truce reduced cross-border attacks, it allowed the Houthis to consolidate their territorial control and strengthen their military capabilities, only to attack Saudi Arabia again.

Negotiation remains the most favourable route towards a lasting settlement. But it faces a fundamental obstacle: the Houthis believe they are winning and have little incentive to compromise.

Nor can Riyadh simply outsource the conflict. The US faces the looming prospect of a renewed confrontation with Iran and is therefore unlikely to have much appetite for opening another front or supporting a prolonged military campaign in Yemen. Saudi Arabia’s defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan may strengthen deterrence and defensive capabilities, but it does not offer a solution to the Houthi threat or Yemen’s underlying political fragmentation.

Saudi Arabia cannot win this war alone, but neither can it outsource its resolution. The lesson of the past decade is that military pressure without a coherent political strategy will only reproduce the conditions that allowed the Houthis to consolidate their position.

A Gulf problem

Instead, a collective Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) response is needed. Yemen and the Houthis have become a collective Gulf security challenge. It would therefore be a mistake to continue treating Yemen primarily as a domestic conflict or a Saudi security problem. 

The attacks on Saudi airports have further demonstrated the vulnerability of critical infrastructure across the GCC to missiles, drones and other asymmetric threats. This exposure is not confined to Saudi Arabia. In January 2022, the Houthis launched attacks on Abu Dhabi’s oil facilities and airport, killing three people and injuring six. This threat is particularly concerning for the Gulf states as most of their economic diversification agendas depend on secure aviation, logistics, tourism, investment and a stable regional environment.

Attacks on Saudi transport infrastructure also threaten the wider Gulf by disrupting vital supply routes. The kingdom’s extensive land connections have become increasingly important and provided alternative supply routes for neighbouring GCC states while the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted. 

Yemen’s economic collapse, water scarcity and demographic pressures also make its stability a long-term Gulf interest. 

The GCC must therefore move beyond expressing support for Saudi Arabia. It should pursue a coordinated strategy that creates a unified GCC agenda directed at strengthening Yemen’s government and establishing a credible political pathway to ending the conflict.

Gulf unity must go beyond condemnation

A collective Gulf response must begin by addressing the divisions that have undermined previous efforts in Yemen. Most importantly, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) must move beyond their damaging confrontation over southern Yemen in early 2026. Despite entering the 2015 intervention as allies, Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have increasingly pursued competing priorities and supported rival Yemeni factions.

Reconciliation requires more than expressions of solidarity following Houthi attacks. The UAE should reconsider its support for southern separatist ambitions and work towards a unified but decentralized Yemen that accommodates southern grievances and competing political interests.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, must reassess its dependence on established Yemeni partners, particularly the Islah Party, whose alleged Muslim Brotherhood connections have long generated Emirati opposition. Riyadh’s reliance on Islah-linked networks has narrowed its political options and contributed to divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.

Both countries must recognize that their competing relationships with Yemeni factions have weakened the very forces they seek to support. Without agreement on Yemen’s political future, renewed military coordination will achieve little.

Gulf coordination must also be matched by a serious reassessment of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

The Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), established in 2022 to replace former president Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi, was intended to unite competing anti-Houthi factions. Yet years of internal rivalries, weak governance, and limited institutional accountability, as well as alleged widespread corruption, have undermined its effectiveness.

Saudi Arabia should continue providing financial support to sustain basic services and prevent economic collapse in government-controlled areas. But this backing should go to the government and cabinet, not the PLC.  

The experience of the Hadi presidency serves as a clear warning that a decade of backing an ineffective leadership did little to strengthen the Yemeni state or reverse Houthi gains. Today, Riyadh cannot afford to repeat that mistake.

A more effective governance structure is essential not only to strengthen the position of anti-Houthi forces but also to provide a credible Yemeni counterpart in any future political settlement.  

Towards a larger Gulf–Yemeni settlement

Although Saudi-Emirati reconciliation is indispensable, a sustainable Gulf strategy must also involve Qatar and Oman.

Qatar should contribute to a more coherent Gulf political approach in Yemen, including through its media influence and relationships with Yemeni actors. Oman, meanwhile, should retain its role as a diplomatic intermediary. Muscat’s channels with the Houthis and preference for mediation make it particularly well placed to facilitate future negotiations without joining military operations.

Related work

Why the Houthis’ Red Sea power play makes Iran even stronger

The ultimate objective should be a Gulf-backed political settlement that preserves a unified but decentralized Yemen and accommodates its competing political constituencies. All factions, including the Houthis, should be able to participate, conditional on verifiable commitments to relinquish heavy weapons and accept a common political framework. This would require sustained Gulf diplomatic and financial support.

After more than a decade of war, the Houthis still control Sanaa, Yemen’s government remains weak and Gulf divisions continue to undermine efforts to end the conflict. Avoiding another prolonged war requires a common Gulf vision, investment in a functioning Yemeni government and a political settlement that addresses the causes of the conflict, rather than merely seeking to contain its consequences.

item.title: The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
item.description:
President Zelenskyy’s allies must show the Russian president that American perfidy won’t alter the course of a war the Kremlin is losing

When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.

These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.

item.title: Maaz Sadaqat sets sights on 2027 World Cup after ODI snub
item.description:
Maaz Sadaqat may have missed out on selection for Pakistan’s upcoming One-day International (ODI) tri-series featuring England and Sri Lanka, but the swashbuckling left-hander has his sights firmly set on next year’s World Cup.

The 21-year-old made a strong impression on the international stage in the recently concluded three-match T20I series against Sri Lanka, scoring consecutive half-centuries in the first two matches to help Pakistan clinch the series.

His performances were more than just individual milestones, signalling a shift towards a more aggressive batting approach in T20 cricket, with Maaz emerging as a key figure in the change.

He scored 50 off 29 balls in the opening match, helping Pakistan recover from an underwhelming powerplay alongside captain Sahibzada Farhan.

In the second T20I, Maaz took the attack to the Sri Lankan bowlers, smashing 96 off 51 balls, including seven sixes and six fours, to come close to a maiden international century.

His impressive run, however, will have to wait for another opportunity to continue in Pakistan colours, with the batter left out of the ODI squad despite having featured in six matches in the format, including his debut, earlier this year.

Maaz had made an immediate impact in only his second ODI against Bangladesh, scoring 75 and taking three wickets with his left-arm spin. However, he struggled to maintain that form in the subsequent home series against Australia in May-June, managing scores of eight, zero and 27 on difficult surfaces.

The reasons behind his omission from the squad for the upcoming tri-series remain unclear. The break, however, offers him an opportunity to refine his game with the 2027 World Cup in mind.

“I am targeting the ODI World Cup and I am preparing for it,” Maaz said in a video interview released by the Pakistan Cricket Board on Thursday. “I have a 15-20-day window coming up which I am going to dedicate to working on myself for the World Cup.”

The youngster, who rose from tape-ball cricket in Peshawar to become a franchise T20 sensation, has continued to build his reputation on the domestic and international circuits. He also struck two centuries in the recently concluded Caribbean Premier League season.

Maaz believes the key to his progress lies in strengthening his natural game rather than focusing excessively on his weaknesses.

“[In training] I try to work as much as I can on my strengths and less on my weaknesses, because if the ball is out of my range, I’d still be able to push it for a single or two,” he said. “However, if it is in my range, then I can hit it for six with my eyes closed.

“If you watch both my CPL and international knocks, I keep a positive intent from the very start.

“And if the ball comes in my range then I don’t spare it. And when a ball is a bit here or there, I try to rotate the strike.”

That clarity of approach also extends to his preferred batting position. Although Maaz has previously said he is open to batting anywhere in the order, he admits he is most comfortable opening the innings.

“I feel the most comfortable playing as an opener,” he said.

A place in Pakistan’s squad for the 2027 World Cup would put Maaz in contention for an opening slot alongside Saim Ayub, who is averaging nearly 47, and experienced campaigner Fakhar Zaman.

Maaz, however, views the competition for places as a challenge rather than a setback.

“Even if I am asked to bat lower in the order, I’ll try to bat so well that they [team management] are forced to push me higher,” he said.

item.title: Windies' Hope worried about excess baggage after landing another Player of the Match award
item.description:
West Indies captain Shai Hope is worried he may have to fork out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India.

The opener’s unbeaten 102 in the fourth Twenty20 International on Wednesday set up a series-levelling win in Hyderabad. He also smashed a century in the second T20 in Ranchi.

Hope has been in sizzling form throughout the tour, hitting two hundreds in the earlier One-Day International leg. And while he was pleased with his performances he said he was struggling to fit his awards in his luggage.

“To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight,” he quipped after West Indies prevailed by 24 runs.

“I think we are going to have some problems going back home.” Hope said getting off to a good start in Hyderabad was key.

“We got 50-plus opening partnership,” he added. “So it was good for us to start innings and then obviously we got that foundation, you can express yourself a bit more in the middle period and then try to give the team the best finish as could as possible.” Hope clobbered nine sixes in his 50-ball knock and drew the admiration of his opponents.

“We need to respect what he has been doing,” India opener Sanju Samson said. “He has been playing some really good cricketing shots, not taking that much risk, and respecting the bowlers as well.” Hope will look to give himself more baggage problems in Saturday’s series decider in Bengaluru.

West Indies will next visit Bangladesh for a two-test series later this month. The hosts will breathe easier knowing Hope is being rested ahead of ODI World Cup qualifiers in February.

item.title: Saudi coalition strikes Yemen oil sites after Houthi attacks
item.description:
YEMEN-SAUDI-IRAN-US-ISRAEL-WAR

The Saudi-led coalition battling the Iran-backed Houthis struck oil sites across western Yemen on Tuesday including in the capital Sanaa, in response to the deadliest attack on the kingdom’s soil in years.

Blasts were heard shortly after in Saudi capital Riyadh and at an oil giant Aramco facility in eastern Saudi Arabia, witnesses and journalists told AFP.

The coalition said it intercepted several Houthi missiles targeting the kingdom, including Riyadh, adding that debris fell in a residential area in Dhahran, which hosts Aramco’s headquarters.

Tuesday’s coalition strikes in Yemen’s Sanaa and the western provinces of Dhamar and Saada targeted facilities used to “supply the war effort” by the Houthis to “threaten the kingdom, Yemen, the southern Red Sea and waterways”, coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote on X.

A powerful explosion then rang out in the Saudi capital, with a phone alert sent to residents saying “the city of Riyadh is facing a hostile aerial threat”.

While walking down a major avenue in Riyadh, a witness told AFP he “saw a projectile cutting across the sky” above a mall, saying it left “a yellowish trail of light followed by a trail of smoke. Then, we heard an explosion.”

“People were calm; no one was speaking. We were scared and all looking up at the sky,” he added, requesting anonymity.

After Houthi strikes on Saudi airports and energy sites in recent days, the coalition issued its first evacuation order in the Yemeni capital since the war flared in July, before attacking the Yemen Petroleum Company facility on Sanaa’s outskirts.

An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV channel said “Saudi aggression” targeted the oil firm.

Renewed threats

A strike on Riyadh’s international airport on Saturday left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.

The Saudi cabinet vowed in a meeting earlier Tuesday, led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, that it “will not allow its security or freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait to be threatened”.

An AFP correspondent reported that many civilians in Sanaa fearing shortages rushed to queue in front of fuel stations after the coalition warning.

The Houthis had earlier issued a new threat to target Riyadh’s international airport, a refinery, and an Aramco facility in Dammam if the strike went ahead, calling for citizens to avoid them.

Many countries have issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam airports.

The Saudi-led coalition has supported Yemen’s government militarily against the Houthis since 2015 in a long-running civil war that has created a dire humanitarian crisis.

Economic woes

Traffic in perennially gridlocked Riyadh was noticeably lighter this week, as remote learning for all schools and work-from-home orders for some companies took effect, according to AFP journalists.

Saudi Arabia faces a major economic contraction this year with GDP expected to shrink 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday, predicting a regional drop over Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran’s chokehold on the Hormuz strait since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.

But the restart in July of Yemen’s frozen war has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.

Houthi attacks have also targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea—Saudi Arabia’s alternative export route.

In Yemen, the renewed fighting was fuelling the risk of infectious disease outbreaks.

Suspected cholera cases tripled there in three weeks, the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that the growing disease burden was straining hospitals already treating war casualties.

‘Behaving very badly’

The Riyadh airport attack had prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

He wrote on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday that “the Houthis are behaving very badly”, accusing them of acting “probably at the behest of Iran”.

“I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!” he wrote, referring to next month’s midterms.

The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.

Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince “that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position”.

item.title: Press Council seeks power to act suo motu and fine journalists
item.description:
The Bangladesh Press Council wants legal authority to act on its own initiative against the publication of news reports that it considers harmful to national integrity, independence or sovereignty, or detrimental to the public interest.

It also believes it should have the power to take similar action against the spread of rumours, fake news and hate speech. In addition, the council wants the law amended to allow it to impose financial penalties on journalists as a form of punishment.

These proposals are outlined in a report submitted by the Press Council to the parliamentary standing committee on the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The committee has yet to discuss the report.

Those familiar with the matter say the Bangladesh Press Council was established to safeguard press freedom and improve and maintain the standards of newspapers and news agencies.

However, the government body has rarely been seen playing a role in protecting press freedom. Instead, during the tenure of the ousted Awami League government, it drafted proposals to amend its governing law in ways that journalists described as an attempt to curtail press freedom.

The powers it is now seeking represent a revival of that earlier effort. Granting the council authority to initiate proceedings on its own would run counter to independent journalism and democratic practice, they argue.

According to sources familiar with the matter, one item on Tuesday’s agenda of the parliamentary standing committee was a discussion on how to make the activities of organisations under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting more dynamic and responsive to the public. In response, 14 organisations under the ministry submitted written proposals to the committee.

It states: “If newspapers, news agencies, editors, publishers or journalists publish or print news or reports that are harmful to the country’s national integrity, independence or sovereignty, contrary to public taste or journalistic codes of conduct, or detrimental to the public interest, or if they spread rumours, fake news or hate speech, the law should empower the council to initiate investigations, issue orders and take necessary action on its own initiative.”

One was titled “Specific proposals to make the overall activities of the Bangladesh Press Council more dynamic and public-oriented”. The report was signed by Press Council Secretary Md Abdus Sabur, a joint secretary of the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

The Press Council’s proposal states that the Press Council Act, enacted in the context of 1974, urgently needs to be updated to keep pace with the current era of free-flowing information and the rapid expansion of modern, technology-driven media.

The aim, it says, is to protect press freedom, improve and maintain media standards, and prevent malpractice in journalism and disinformation. To achieve this, the law should incorporate additional powers and areas of jurisdiction. The proposal lists 19 such powers.

They include registering journalists and issuing them certificates, setting minimum educational qualifications, bringing online news outlets under the council’s jurisdiction, establishing a code of conduct for journalists, and investigating attacks on or obstruction of independent journalism while providing protection to those affected.

The council also proposes that it be authorised to collect a levy or contribution from newspapers based on their circulation to ensure its financial self-sufficiency.

The Press Council Act was also slated for amendment under the Awami League government, which was ousted in the July mass uprising. In June 2022, the Cabinet gave in-principle approval to a draft amendment. The law was ultimately not amended.

NOAB President and Manabzamin chief editor Matiur Rahman ChowdhuryIf the Press Council or any other institution were given the power to act on its own initiative, there would be little need for the courts and the legal process.

At the time, the proposed changes included financial penalties and the power to take cognisance of offences on the council’s own initiative. The draft initially proposed fines of up to Tk 1 million, but the specific amount was removed when the Cabinet granted its in-principle approval.

The initiative drew criticism during the Awami League’s tenure. The Newspaper Owners’ Association of Bangladesh (NOAB) objected to the proposals, saying, “The proposed amendments are vague and therefore open to abuse. In particular, they refer to matters harmful to or derogatory towards the security, independence and sovereignty of the state, but provide no precise interpretation of these terms.”

Asked about the Press Council’s proposals to the parliamentary standing committee, NOAB President and Manabzamin chief editor Matiur Rahman Chowdhury told Prothom Alo that if the Press Council or any other institution were given the power to act on its own initiative, there would be little need for the courts and the legal process.

The way these legal powers are being proposed would obstruct democratic practice and independent journalism, he said. Attempts were made to introduce similar provisions under the Awami League government. It would be unfortunate if the same effort were repeated now.

He added that the council was unable to exercise even the powers it already possessed. Many people regarded it as a toothless institution, he said, and any amendment to the law must be preceded by consultations with stakeholders.

In what circumstances does the council want to investigate on its own initiative?

The report says the Press Council should be empowered to initiate investigations and take appropriate action in certain circumstances.

It states: “If newspapers, news agencies, editors, publishers or journalists publish or print news or reports that are harmful to the country’s national integrity, independence or sovereignty, contrary to public taste or journalistic codes of conduct, or detrimental to the public interest, or if they spread rumours, fake news or hate speech, the law should empower the council to initiate investigations, issue orders and take necessary action on its own initiative.”

The report further says the council should be authorised to investigate and order necessary protective measures when the freedom to publish news or practise independent journalism is obstructed, or when journalists face attacks or mob violence.

Such action could follow a complaint by the publisher or editor of an affected newspaper, or be initiated by the council itself when there are credible grounds to believe that press freedom has been violated.

The council has also proposed a provision to expedite the resolution of complaints. Under the proposed procedure, when an aggrieved person files a complaint, the council would initially direct the editor of the newspaper concerned to resolve the matter. The editor would then discuss the complaint with the complainant and seek a settlement.

The Press Council currently operates as a quasi-judicial body. It says a judge of district judge rank should be included as a member and that the council should be given exclusive authority to adjudicate matters involving journalists’ rights and professional misconduct.

The report also proposes effective legal provisions allowing financial penalties for publishing false or harassing reports, material that violates journalistic ethics or public taste, or content that breaches the code of conduct.

Emphasising the need for a code of conduct for journalists, the proposal argues that, because compliance is not mandatory, journalists are not sufficiently conscious of the need to uphold professional ethics, publish objective news and practise responsible journalism. It therefore recommends adding a provision requiring the code to be published in the official gazette. The council itself would draft the code.

The report also takes issue with journalists working in other professions simultaneously. It describes this as a clear violation of journalistic principles and ethics and a serious form of professional misconduct.

Holding two or more jobs at the same time, it argues, undermines the professional standards and dignity of journalism. The council says this restriction should be explicitly incorporated into the law.

Former head of the Media Reform Commission Kamal Ahmed, asked about the proposals, said there appeared to be a misconception that the Press Council was a judicial institution. It is an organisation under the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, he said, and should not be granted the power to issue orders on its own initiative.

He also noted that the proposal did not address bringing broadcast media under the Press Council’s jurisdiction. “Will a separate authority be established for that purpose?” he asked.

Kamal Ahmed said the current government should adopt the proposals made by the Media Reform Commission. Instead, the latest proposals selectively retain certain elements, he argued.

Kamal Ahmed further said that reviving an ineffective institution such as the Press Council in this way would not benefit the media. Rather, it should be abolished and replaced with the commission promised by the BNP, he said, a body that would be independent and permanent.

item.title: Bangladesh calls for global treaty to protect victims of crimes against humanity
item.description:
Bangladesh has called for a strong international convention to prevent and punish crimes against humanity, urging special recognition and support for countries hosting victims of such atrocities.
Addressing the Sixth Committee of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Bangladesh delegate Muhammad Nawshad Zamir proposed three key provisions for the convention: cooperation in preserving evidence and protecting witnesses in receiving States; support for survivors, including access to justice at national and international levels; and international solidarity in sharing the burden borne by host countries.
Citing Bangladesh’s experience sheltering over 1 million Rohingyas forcibly displaced from Myanmar, he stressed that countries receiving victims must be integral to international accountability mechanisms, according to the Permanent Mission of Bangladesh to the United Nations in New York.
Referring to Bangladesh’s 2024 uprising, Zamir cited a UN report estimating that up to 1,400 people, including children, were killed, calling for investigations into possible crimes against humanity.
Bangladesh also advocated universal jurisdiction, stronger extradition mechanisms and an end to impunity, while emphasising prevention and justice for women and children.
The Bangladesh delegate urged that the convention complement the Rome Statute and uphold the International Criminal Court’s independence.
“A convention diluted until it offends no one will protect no one,” he warned.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 5th globally in air pollution
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 5th among the world's most polluted cities on Wednesday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 175 at 10:20am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
Singapore in Singapore ranked first with an AQI score of 194, while Delhi in India ranked second with a score of 180, followed by Kuala Lumpur in Malaysia in third place with an AQI score of 177.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered 'unhealthy for sensitive groups', while 151 to 200 is classified as 'unhealthy'. A reading between 201 and 300 is considered 'very unhealthy', while levels above 301 are deemed 'hazardous', posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Budhi Gandaki flood poses no direct threat to Bangladesh, but it holds lessons for early warning
item.description:
Nepal has experienced two major floods within a short span of time. The flood in August was particularly devastating. The most recent one occurred on 11 October.

Such disasters in the Himalayan foothills are a warning not only for Nepal but also for other South Asian countries. Saswata Sanyal, intervention manager in ICIMOD’s Disaster Risk Reduction Division, spoke to Prothom Alo about the causes of the floods, early warning systems and the lessons the region can learn. The interview was conducted by Partha Shankar Saha.

Two major floods have hit Nepal within a relatively short period. Such disasters have long occurred because of the geological characteristics of the Himalayas. How can we determine whether climate warming is increasing the frequency or intensity of these floods? What evidence can help establish this?

Saswata Sanyal: The Himalayas are a relatively young mountain range with steep slopes and high seismic activity and they have a long history of both types of disasters. The same Bhotekoshi corridor was hit in July 2025. At that time, NDRRMA reported a glacial lake outburst originating in the upper catchment.

The two events in 2026 also had different causes. The Rasuwa–Gyirong flood in August began with a high-altitude rock–ice collapse. In the case of the Budhi Gandaki River flood, the NDRRMA has said provisionally that a landslide blocked the flow of a tributary. The dam later broke, triggering the flood. No link between this event and glaciers or ice has yet been established.

Warming primarily increases risks in high mountain areas through glacier thinning, permafrost thaw and increased meltwater. To distinguish these effects from geological hazards, several types of evidence are needed:

  • Using previous satellite data to compile a record of disasters over several decades, while correcting for gaps and biases in data collection;

  • Regularly measuring changes in land and glacier elevation in the same areas, and monitoring landslide-prone slopes and glaciers using radar-based InSAR technology;

  • Temperature and permafrost records at source elevations;

  • Rather than directly attributing an individual disaster to climate change, examining the relationship between warming and the hazardous conditions that developed before the event.

Another reason for the increase in damage is the growth of settlements, roads and hydropower plants along river valleys. As a result, the number of people living in vulnerable areas and the amount of infrastructure exposed to these hazards have also increased.

Reports say residents began warning one another around 4:45 am, while the first official warning came later and mass SMS alerts were sent at 6:40 am. What failed in the official warning chain, and how can community reports be incorporated quickly into a trusted, formal alert system?

Saswata Sanyal: On 11 October, residents began alerting one another at about 4:45 am. The Arughat police post issued the first official warning at 5:30 am. FFD and NDRRMA received initial reports around 6:00 am and sent mass SMS at 6:40 am. The nearest automatic water-level sensor is at Arughat, about 65 km downstream of the source, so the FFD relied on reports from residents and officials.

Once the warning system was activated, the dissemination of alerts worked properly. The question is not what failed, but it was to verify the detection, and the hand-off from a credible field report to an authorised alert. The idea is to not give false alerts from the government as well.

In remote mountain valleys with limited monitoring, what combination of local phone networks, river sensors, satellite observation and other tools could provide useful warning time for both landslide-dam outburst floods and glacial lake outburst floods?

Saswata Sanyal: Warning time comes from detecting the hazard high in the catchment and acting fast. A layered system works best:

  • Satellite screening: identifies growing lakes, slope creep and new landslide dams weeks to months ahead;

  • Seismic detection: flags large collapses within minutes;

  • Upstream network of sensors: placed at known glacial lakes and at newly formed dams once detected a network of different kind of sensors like cameras, microphone, geophones, wire sensors to focus on where exactly the breach is;

  • Trigger mechanism and sacrificial infrastructure: Rate of rise of water takes place faster than the data is transmitted to the server. Therefore, rate-of-rise can’t be captured. Additionally, if the sensors stop transmitting that should also trigger alerts as it means they have been washed away. On 11th Oct we saw the water level drop as well uncharacteristically, this should also trigger alerts as it mean that there might have been a major landslide upstream. The trigger mechanism needs to be overhauled;

  • Trained phone observers with satellite or radio backup: for when mobile towers fail.

Glacial lakes are largely known sites and can be instrumented. Landslide dams appear without notice, so they need rapid detection.

The flood damaged homes, bridges, trails and a hydropower construction site. Do current planning and engineering rules adequately account for fast-moving water carrying mud, rocks and debris? What changes are most urgent in the siting and protection of settlements and infrastructure?

Saswata Sanyal: Not adequately for these kind of impact or hazards. Infrastructure is typically designed for clear-water floods of a given return period. The government RDNA puts recovery needs at about USD 4.74 billion, around 75 per cent of it for infrastructure. Most urgent changes:

  • Multi-hazard risk informed land-use zoning to guide reconstruction, so recovery funds do not rebuild exposure;

  • Relocating construction camps, worker housing and border posts off valley floors;

  • Checking critical assets against debris-flow and outburst scenarios;

  • hydropower licence conditions covering upstream multi-hazard risk monitoring and evacuation plans;

  • Debris-tolerant river crossings.

For readers in Bangladesh, how should the Budhi Gandaki flood’s significance be understood? Is there any direct downstream concern beyond Nepal, or are the main lessons for Bangladesh about preparedness, monitoring and cooperation across Himalayan river basins?

Saswata Sanyal: There is no direct physical threat to Bangladesh. The Budhi Gandaki joins the Trishuli, which flows into the Narayani/Gandak and then the Ganges. Even the much larger August flood had attenuated to a routine level by Devghat in southern Nepal.

The relevance for Bangladesh lies in the lessons from Nepal’s gaps in detection, warning and planning:

  • Layered warning systems for fast-onset floods, combining satellite screening, seismic detection and upstream sensors, rather than relying only on downstream gauges designed for slow, rainfall-driven rises;

  • Alert triggers that respond to a sharp rate of rise, an unusual drop in water level or sensors going offline, not only to fixed danger levels;

  • A fast, verified hand-off from community reports to official alerts, where Bangladesh’s Cyclone Preparedness Programme is itself a model for the region;

  • Multi-hazard, risk-informed siting and design of riverside settlements, embankments and crossings, so that reconstruction does not rebuild exposure;

  • Timely, real-time upstream hydrological data, alongside longer-term research on sediment pulses moving through shared river systems.

These are shared risks across the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Data-sharing arrangements are for governments to agree, with common standards developed regionally.

Based on the recent floods, what are the three most urgent steps Nepal and regional agencies should take before the next high-impact event—and who needs to lead each step?

Saswata Sanyal: Drawing on the lessons above, three steps stand out:

Warning: a national alert-to-action protocol that links each warning level to fixed duties for every tier of government and every actor on a river, with a fast, verified route from community and field reports to pre-authorised alerts. Lead: NDRRMA, with DHM/FFD and local governments.

Detection: satellite screening of glacial lakes, unstable slopes and new landslide dams, starting with the most exposed river corridors, backed by upstream sensors and alert triggers that respond to rate of rise, sudden drops in water level and sensors going offline. Lead: DHM with universities and research institutes; ICIMOD supporting methods, regional data and training.

Planning and cooperation: multi-hazard, risk-informed zoning to guide reconstruction, debris-flow and outburst checks on critical assets, and hydropower licence conditions covering upstream multi-hazard monitoring and evacuation plans, alongside corridor-based data-sharing and warning arrangements with neighbouring countries. Lead: NDRRMA and local governments for zoning; the Department of Electricity Development for hydropower licences; governments through bilateral mechanisms for information-sharing, with ICIMOD and WMO supporting regional standards and platforms.

item.title: Parliamentary committee asks govt to identify officials obstructing its work
item.description:
A parliamentary committee has recommended that the Ministry of Public Administration identify and take necessary action against those obstructing or neglecting the current government’s activities aimed at implementing the policy of “Bangladesh first”.

The recommendation was made at a meeting of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Public Administration at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban on Wednesday. The committee also recommended investigating the projects which were progressing slowly.

The information was disclosed in a press release issued by the Parliament Secretariat after the meeting. The committee was briefed on the activities of offices and agencies under the Ministry of Public Administration.

It advised all concerned to coordinate their activities at the field level to implement the 31-point reform agenda for state reform by bringing about a change in mindset.

Committee Chairman Sayeed Ahmed said that any legal, administrative or practical obstacles to implementing a decision must be brought to the committee’s attention. Necessary information, relevant documents and the actual circumstances must be presented without concealing anything.

He said public services must be made easier and faster, and accountability must be ensured. Digital services and the use of information technology can save citizens’ time, money and effort. Therefore, effective use of technology in service delivery must be ensured, and appropriate action must be taken against irregularities.

The committee chairman further said, “To solve problems, we must move beyond our traditional mindset and work with a spirit of accountability, transparency and cooperation. Do not forget that you are employees of the Republic. You do not belong to any party, individual or group. Do not consider this committee an adversary; it is a committee for all of us.”

The meeting was chaired by Sayeed Ahmed. Among the committee members who attended were State Minister for Public Administration Md Abdul Bari, ABM Ashraf Uddin (Nizan), Shahjahan Chowdhury, Amirul Islam Khan, Fakhr Uddin Ahmed, Rehena Akter and Md Nurul Islam.

item.title: FBI arrests and investigates this OpenAI engineer over a ‘sophisticated listening device’
item.description:
An engineer at OpenAI has been charged with secretly installing a recording device inside a conference room in what officials said Tuesday was an effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology.

The employee, identified as a 35-year-old Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested Friday, a week after the ChatGPT maker discovered an audio recording device hidden inside a company conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.

The complaint did not identify the company, but the company confirmed in a separate statement that it had discovered a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices,” reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee.

“We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

The complaint does not detail what Alfozan might have wanted to do with any captured communications, but the company said the device was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio monitoring capabilities. OpenAI said it had evidence the employee planned to place other listening devices throughout other parts of the office building for the purpose of recording meetings.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Alfozan made his first court appearance Tuesday on a charge of using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. It was not immediately clear if he had a lawyer who could speak on his behalf. He is due back in court on Oct. 19.

The recording device was found September 30 concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to the complaint.

Though the conference room where the recording device was found did not have a security camera at the time the object was installed, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed that Alfozan was near the conference room on nearly a dozen occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space or participate in meetings there, the complaint says.

The company subsequently added a camera to the room that last week captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been installed, according to the FBI.

The complaint also alleges that he used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.

Days before his arrest last week, the complaint says, Alfozan left behind an unattended bag in a different room that, when opened by OpenAI personnel, was found to contain his wallet, identification and another recording device similar to the one placed in the conference room.

—Eric Tucker, Associated Press

item.title: Bank of America stock falls in the wake of a historic $1.2 billion fine after it failed to report financial crime
item.description:
Bank of America has been fined over $1.2 billion for violating anti-money-laundering and sanction laws. 

On Tuesday, October 13, the U.S. Department of the Treasury handed down the fine, stating that Bank of America had failed to report over $5 billion in “suspicious activity” to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN). 

Over $1 billion of the activity was “national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks, including suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese Money Laundering Networks, fraud, and potential trade-based money laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border,” the Treasury stated in its announcement. 

“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risk,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

Third largest in history

The $1.2 billion fine is the Treasury Department’s third largest in its history. In 2023, it fined Binance $3.4 billion and, a year later, fined TD Bank $1.3 billion. 

The total figure includes a $750 million fine from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)—the largest in its history—for having an “ineffective” anti-money laundering program. 

It also comprised an $11.6 million settlement agreement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). While this is the smallest part of the fine, the 475 “apparent violations of sanction programs” are quite notable. These sanctions were against Russia, Iran, global terrorism, and narcotics, among other significant areas. 

According to the Treasury, “these apparent violations occurred when Bank of America channeled correspondent banking payments through blocked banks due to technical and human error.”

“We are responsible for getting it right”

Reached for comment by Fast Company, a Bank of America spokesperson said the financial services giant has invested “billions of dollars” in financial crime and is committed to addressing the issues raised by U.S. regulators.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “We worked with regulators to reach these penalty resolutions stemming from violations cited in the previously reported 2024 OCC Consent Order and FinCEN’s investigation.”

Stock down after third-quarter earnings

Shares of Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC) were down more than 8% on Wednesday following the fine and an early-morning earnings report.

The company reported $30.12 billion in revenue for quarter three, falling short of Wall Street’s predicted $30.69 billion, according to consensus estimates cited by CNBC.

“Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share,” Bank of America’s statement said. “We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base.”

item.title: Why Does Saudi Arabia Struggle to Stop Houthi Attacks?
The ceasefire that keeps killing children: Gaza one year on
Washington Cannot Outsource Saudi Security to the Mecca Pact
item.description:
The Houthis have significantly escalated their airstrike campaign targeting civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, with two consecutive attacks at Riyadh’s international airport, killing 12 and injuring 300 others between October 10 and 11. The Houthis’ deadly strike campaign has exposed an uncomfortable truth that Saudi Arabia’s newest defense alliance cannot yet guarantee its security. Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani leaders activated the Mecca Pact on October 5, but the Riyadh airport attacks demonstrated how little a collective-defense declaration means to an adversary willing to keep firing. Riyadh needs more than diplomatic solidarity and bare-minimum defense support, which are not willing to undertake kinetic engagements with the Houthis. Washington should expand military assistance to Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognized government without rushing into another open-ended bombing campaign. The United States has greater strategic interests at stake than either Ankara or Islamabad, and capabilities the new pact cannot quickly replicate.

Saudi Energy Security Is American Security

Saudi Arabia remains a central American security partner and an indispensable player in global energy markets. With Iranian attacks and disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, the kingdom’s East-West Pipeline has become a critical alternative for moving crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The pipeline throughput reportedly reached approximately 5.8 million barrels per day in early October, while roughly four million barrels per day have been rerouted around Hormuz.

This arrangement, however, remains vulnerable to external attacks that can disrupt the flow of energy from the Middle East. Drone attacks forced a temporary pipeline shutdown in late September, although Saudi Arabia attributed those strikes to Iran-backed Iraqi militias. The Houthis have separately attacked and threatened Saudi energy facilities. And despite a September rebound to 16.3 million barrels per day, Middle Eastern crude exports remained below their prewar level of 19.5 million. A prolonged Saudi-Houthi war could jeopardize the infrastructure and confidence sustaining that fragile recovery.

Security threats to Saudi Arabia also complicate ongoing and future diplomatic gains with Riyadh, especially considering President Donald Trump’s vision to have Saudi Arabia join the Abraham Accords. The US-Saudi civilian nuclear cooperation agreement, signed in July and submitted for congressional review in August, promises a long-term economic and strategic relationship. While its proliferation safeguards deserve rigorous scrutiny, escalating security threats could complicate implementation and diminish Washington’s influence over Saudi nuclear choices. Pakistan and Turkey have interests in Saudi stability; the United States has energy, maritime, defense-industrial, and nonproliferation interests simultaneously.

Pakistan Has Too Many Fronts of Its Own

The pact’s most acute capacity problem lies in Pakistan. Islamabad must contain the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Baloch separatist violence while guarding a contested frontier with Afghanistan and maintaining forces opposite India. These are not hypothetical distractions but serious battlefield challenges for Islamabad, which is fighting on multiple fronts simultaneously. Pakistan conducted airstrikes inside Afghanistan on October 1, amid recurring border clashes. On October 11, Islamabad imposed emergency rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, citing worsening militancy, although the opposition disputes the justification. Additionally, the India frontier remains an enduring contingency that Pakistani planners cannot discount. This threat landscape will create serious bandwidth issues for Pakistan’s military in the immediate to near term, further limiting Islamabad’s support for Riyadh.

Pakistan’s armed forces can provide specialized assistance abroad, but sustained expeditionary commitments require personnel, logistics, and strategic attention. Pakistani officials have dismissed Western media reports of its troop presence in government-controlled territories of Yemen. Still, the death of a Pakistani driver in a Houthi drone strike in Marib, Yemen, has brought Pakistan’s actual role within the defense pact under scrutiny—whether Islamabad is taking up a direct combat role alongside the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces on the ground. On the other hand, Turkey has formidable drones, electronic-warfare expertise, and NATO experience, but its priorities extend from Syria and Iraq to the Eastern Mediterranean. Neither country should be dismissed as a partner, and neither should be treated as an unlimited strategic reserve for a war with no clear end date.

Bab al-Mandeb Is Washington’s Problem Too

The constant threat of disrupting commercial vessel traffic in the Red Sea makes American restraint increasingly difficult. Washington and the Houthis have recently reached an understanding that the group will not target non-Saudi ships in the Red Sea given that the United States does not undertake kinetic strikes targeting Houthi infrastructure in Yemen. This is a non-binding understanding and dangerously shortsighted, which offers no permanent guarantee that the Houthis would never threaten Bab al-Mandeb again. If the Houthis begin losing territory rapidly to the government forces, they are highly likely to use every means possible to threaten commercial vessels in the Red Sea. This is right out of their counterpart Iran’s coercion playbook around Hormuz, illustrating the leverage a regional actor can extract from a chokepoint without maintaining a total blockade.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces have made meaningful gains along the western coast of Yemen over the past week. The anti-Houthi coalition of Yemeni forces reportedly retook Perim Island and al Aradi after securing Jabal Kahbub, an operationally significant hilltop which overlooks the frontlines between the Houthi rebels and government forces. Saudi Close Air Support helped enable the counteroffensive, which was partially successful because Houthi positions elsewhere on the Red Sea coast still pose threats against commercial shipping. Bottom line is that the loss of terrain nearest the strait does not eliminate the maritime risk.

Conclusion

Limited tactical success to the credit of Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces should not be conflated with larger operational achievements against the Houthis. Washington should therefore expand real-time targeting support, aerial refueling, integrated air and missile defense, counter-drone capabilities, and maritime surveillance. It should help Saudi and Yemeni forces protect infrastructure and hold recovered ground, while keeping the threshold for direct US strikes explicit: demonstrable threats to American forces, international navigation, or sustained attacks that overwhelm partner defenses. Any strikes must be narrowly targeted, legally justified, and paired with a diplomatic off-ramp.

There is precedent, but also a warning. During Operation Rough Rider, US forces struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets between March and May 2025. The campaign ended in May without destroying the movement but severely degraded the group’s missile production infrastructure. Washington knows how to hit Houthi infrastructure, a task which Turkey and Pakistan are hesitant to and most likely incapable of undertaking. Bipartisan backing for Saudi defense would strengthen this approach, but it cannot compensate for strategic passivity. The Mecca partners can share the burden, but they cannot yet carry it alone. America should neither outsource Saudi security to an untested pact nor inherit Yemen’s entire war. Washington must provide the military support necessary to safeguard its strategic interests while making clear that further Houthi escalation will invite a more forceful, direct US military response.

item.title: The Next War of Attrition is in Yemen
item.description:
Battlefield dynamics in Yemen shift quickly, but Houthi aims do not. A movement organized around radical ideology and perpetual conflict now shares a border with a state organized around modernization and prosperity. Saudi Arabia and the Houthis both have formidable but very different military capabilities, and neither can force a quick decision on the other. That is the recipe for a long war of attrition. The closest precedent is the war in Ukraine, to which the Yemen war is increasingly linked, and which may be instructive for the Kingdom on how best to prepare.

There is also a parallel to be made with the related conflict between Iran and the United States, the fallout from which has severely affected the GCC countries, including Saudi Arabia. Essentially, we are witnessing the leverage of a lesser military force when that party has a much higher threshold for pain and disruption than the stronger party. Iran and the Houthis are both betting that the Saudis are sufficiently anxious to hold on to their peaceful model of business, tourism, energy and investment to settle at almost any price and end the present conflict.

The Houthi mindset

The Houthi ideological program is anti-Saudi, anti-American, anti-Israel, anti-democratic, anti-liberal and antisemitic. It has long cast the Saudi monarchy as an American-Israeli puppet unworthy of the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques. Some of this is personal: The father of Abdelmalek al-Houthi, the group's leader, clashed for years with Saudi-backed clerics and was rumored to have been targeted for assassination at their behest.

But the grievances against the Kingdom also has a territorial dimension. In the 1934 Treaty of Taif,

Imam Yahya of northern Yemen settled the border with the Saudi state and ceded Jizan, Asir, and Najran provinces. The Houthis, who present themselves somewhat ambiguously as heirs to the imamate, have revived claims to all three provinces. The purpose is to stoke resentment of the Saudis and to leave the Kingdom's southern border unsettled. This territorial dimension intersects with the allegation that the Saudis are not fit to control Mecca and Medina: Abdelmalik recently reiterated that Mecca belongs to the Islamic Umma, rather than being a province of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis implicitly – and sometimes explicitly – claim the whole of the southern half of the Arabian Peninsula, “from Mecca to Mahra”.

The deeper reason the Houthis cannot stop is structural. The Houthis depend on mobilization, and for a movement of that kind peace is a threat rather than a reward. Conflict is what holds the project together, as it justifies extracting resources from an impoverished population, excuses unpaid salaries and collapsed services, and lets the security apparatus treat every critic as a collaborator. For a deeply unpopular regime, war with Saudi Arabia and its local Yemeni partners is the most useful conflict available and could yield significant returns if the Houthis can extract concessions at the negotiating table. It was already clear during Ambassador Fitton-Brown’s period of responsibility for Yemen that the perverse incentives of the war economy meant that Houthi negotiator Muhammad Abdelsalam was viewed with suspicion by Houthi field commanders, who were benefitting from the war economy and associated “respect”, and had no interest in being transformed into administrators with responsibility to balance their power.

The Houthi menu

The Houthis approach is predatory: isolate each victim and deal with it alone. They pursue bilateral deals that peel off potential adversaries, and calibrate each attack so the victim would conclude that a limited response is cheaper than a sustained one. They have cultivated the sense that they are somebody else's problem, Israel's when they fire missiles at Eilat, Riyadh's when they strike Abha, etc. A decade on, the Houthis have have attacked many different states, and yet no one has owned the problem.

It is troubling that US negotiators have recently sat with the Houthis in Muscat and apparently taken at face value Houthi assurances that their quarrel is only with the Saudis, not with American – or even the Israelis! All this while threatening the US economy and risking the lives of US nationals at civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom.

In the current round of fighting, the Houthis have three key options for escalation.

The first is domestic expansion within Yemen. It is the least risky for the regime because it stays within a conflict the world has learned to ignore. New territory brings new populations to tax, new ports and crossings to control, and new momentum to display at home. The drawback is that this also pushes the Zaidi Houthis deeper and deeper into Shafa’I (Sunni) territory, where the population is hostile to their agenda.

The second option is maritime. Attacks on commercial vessels and Saudi tankers in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab inflict harm, especially in the economic realm, and they are extremely difficult to deter and defend against. The drawback is that shipping is a global interest, albeit somewhat elastic, and so a sustained campaign against it may invite the involvement of states with maritime commercial interests that would otherwise stay out of a Saudi-Houthi war. It also, by violating the Law of the Sea, provides an unimpeachable legal basis to build an international military coalition against them.

The third option, targeting civilian aviation, is the riskiest. A recent Houthi attack, on October 10, killed at least twelve people in the deadliest attack on the Kingdom in more than a decade. One US national was among the dead. The strikes came with a threat to airlines, "for the last time," to stay out of Saudi airspace. This type of attack is probably the most likely to galvanize an international coalition and demonstrates that the Houthis have an extremely high appetite for risk.

The Houthis are testing how far they can take this. Downing a passenger aircraft would almost certainly bring the overwhelming response, including direct American strikes, that the Houthis have spent recent decades seeking to avoid (albeit with an imperfect record). The threat alone can inflict some damage to Saudi Arabia, so the threats will continue. Whether the Houthis will continue or even take escalation in this realm even further will depend on whether they believe anyone would make them pay.

The wars are already connected

It might be tempting to treat the Russia-Ukraine and Houthi-Saudi comparison as merely illustrative, but the two wars are materially linked in both directions.

Russia’s involvement with the Houthis is the most direct link thus far. By mid-2024, Russia had recruited hundreds, possibly even thousands, of Yemeni men for the Ukrainian front through a Houthi-linked network operating out of Oman. Also, during the Houthi Red Sea campaign of 2023 to 2025, Russia reportedly passed satellite targeting data to the Houthis. And the Shahed-136 that Iran supplied to Russia, which Russia now mass-produces and improved upon, belongs to the same family of weapon the Houthis fire at Saudi infrastructure. Russian innovation may yet flow back through Tehran to Sanaa.

Russia’s public posture toward the Houthi problem has been one of ostensible concern. In September, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov called Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian targets “unacceptable,” and President Putin and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman discussed freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab by phone. Riyadh should not mistake this for neutrality: Moscow treats the Houthis as a pawn in a larger game.

The mechanism is not complicated. A crisis on the Arabian Peninsula drains Western attention and, perhaps more importantly, Western munitions. In late March, the Pentagon was reported to be weighing whether to divert air defense interceptors bought for Ukraine to the Middle East, because the war with Iran was straining stocks of critical American munitions. This is the outcome Moscow has been working toward since it abstained on the 2015 arms embargo against the Houthis and then spent a decade obstructing the UN panel that documented its violations. Russia does not need the Houthis to win; it needs them to keep fighting. It makes a similar calculation over supporting continuing Iranian resistance to the Americans.

The link is starting to run the other way too. Kyiv’s growing ties with Saudi Arabia are more recent but no less consequential. On March 27, the two countries signed a defense cooperation agreement centered on counter-drone expertise. More than two hundred Ukrainian anti-drone specialists are now deployed in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, and Riyadh is reportedly negotiating a large purchase of Ukrainian interceptor drones that cost between one and three thousand dollars each. Until recently Riyadh was deepening ties with Moscow through OPEC+ and BRICS, and yet it is now importing Ukrainian expertise to defend against weapons Moscow helped perfect.

Saudi Arabia's dilemma

As in Eastern Europe, no quick decision is likely in the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The Houthis cannot be bombed out of Sanaa, as the coalition learned between 2015 and 2022. While the Yemeni government’s counteroffensive along the coast has stabilized the front and claimed gains around Mokha, it remains a long way from the capital. That leaves Riyadh with three paths, none of them are likely to be easy.

The first is appeasement, which would feed the movement. Since June, the Houthis have demanded a deal that lifts the blockade on their ports and airports and restores the flow of cash into Sanaa. Such a deal would ease the regime’s revenue crisis and pay for its next tranche of weapons. The Kingdom tried a version of this approach after 2022, and the result is the war it is fighting now.

The second is deterrence, which fails against an adversary that seeks out perpetual conflict. Deterrence assumes an enemy that weighs costs and benefits in measurements that the Saudis understand, and that appears not to be the case. For a movement like the Houthis whose legitimacy rests on “resistance,” conflict is not only a hazard but also a realization of an extremist aspiration.

The third is defeating the Houthis outright, which means returning to a war Saudi Arabia already fought and abandoned. A strategy that could succeed does exist: cut Houthi supply lines of cash and other material while backing a unified Yemeni ground campaign under a single command. But this will require sustained pressure over time in order to crack the Houthi defenses and then ultimately the regime.

Attrition, then, is the most reasonable path forward. The question is not whether Saudi Arabia will be in a long war but whether it will be prepared for one. Attrition is survivable for the side that innovates and devastating for the side that assumes the war will end in a quick and decisive maneuver. The length of the war also introduces uncertainties about changes in the posture of allies, especially the US. There is a need to bake in bipartisan agreement in Washington, DC, that it is a US national security interest to ensure that the Saudis, and the Internationally Recognized Government of Yemen, and the Law of the Sea prevail in this conflict.

Two Ukrainian lessons

Ukraine survived attrition against a far larger adversary for two reasons, and both apply to Riyadh.

The first is adaptation. It built a drone industry from almost nothing into one producing millions of systems a year, fielded interceptor drones costing a small fraction of a Patriot missile, and compressed production and procurement timelines.

The Saudi-Ukranian March agreement imports some of that expertise but may not necessarily transfer all of the knowledge necessary to built its own industry. A defense that depends on imports from a country at war is precarious at the best of times.

Riyadh has the money and the stated intent, and Vision 2030 set a goal of localizing half of military spending by the end of the decade. But localization so far has meant licensed assembly of foreign designs rather than innovation under fire. The Kingdom has not reached a wartime tempo in which a new counter-drone system is conceived, tested against live Houthi attacks, and fielded within weeks. That is the capability Ukraine built and Saudi Arabia lacks.

The second lesson is diplomatic. Ukraine did not survive alone. It built a coalition of dozens of states that supplied weapons, trained its forces, financed its budget, and shared intelligence. For the Houthis, a coalition of this kind is the worst possible development, and it is exactly what their strategy of isolating victims and claiming false symmetry is meant to prevent.

The current war gives Riyadh the chance to build one, but the pieces remain fragmented. Ukraine's example is that a coalition does not assemble itself. It must be rallied, placed under a single command, and given a shared objective beyond absorbing attacks. The Houthis' own escalation, which has now killed citizens of a dozen countries at a single airport, is doing part of that work for Riyadh. The Kingdom's task is to turn condemnation into commitment before the moment passes.

So what would this coalition look like? The Saudis already have a maritime group of 14 that opposes Houthi blackmail against them in the Red Sea. But the US, UAE, UK and the other European powers are not part of it. With US leadership and assistance, this needs to be remedied. This is achievable, on the basis of three compelling legal bases: enforcement of the Law of the Sea; the legitimacy of the Yemeni government (and illegitimacy of the Houthis); and the legitimate defense and self-defense of Saudi Arabia.
